title: COP31 ends without a deal
transcript:
Speaker 1: Bill Hare is a physicist and climate scientist and former lead author of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and he is the CEO of the non-profit Policy Institute Climate Analytics.
Speaker 2: Well, look, I think we've seen a pretty remarkable set of events at the cop in Turkey.
Speaker 2: Um, the main thing for me is that the cover decision, the main decision has been blocked by a whole bunch of countries who are very unhappy about the fact that it didn't mention the transition away from fossil fuels.
Speaker 2: The need for a roadmap to get out of fossil fuels is absolutely critical if we're going to limit global warming.
Speaker 2: And, uh, it's really great to have seen a whole lot of countries actually stand up and say no to fossil fuel interests.
Speaker 1: You've watched the talks from the sidelines, uh, across the Fortnite.
Speaker 1: At what point do you think things really started to break down?
Speaker 2: Well, I think the last 72 hours began to see things unravel.
Speaker 2: It became clear that the presidency text was not going to meet the needs of more than a 100 plus countries to transition away from fossil fuels, to keep out critical language on carbon capture and storage and some other things.
Speaker 2: So, I think by early this morning it was quite clear to me that, uh, this was not going to survive.
Speaker 2: There was going to be a really big push back and there was a risk of the whole cop collapsing.
Speaker 1: An EU representative accused some of the oil states of hijacking the talks.
Speaker 1: What do you think?
Speaker 2: Well, look, the oil states have been hijacking these talks for 30 years.
Speaker 2: So, for me, that's nothing new.
Speaker 2: I think what was really new is a line in the sand has emerged now, where countries have said enough is enough.
Speaker 2: Multilateralism is not about a few countries bullying others, it's about all of us, smaller countries, having an equal say and protecting ourselves from dangers like global warming.
Speaker 2: The European Union, of course, um, is not without our criticism in this whole process.
Speaker 2: It really faltered a little on finance, but the big story is a block on language that did not mention fossil fuels.
Speaker 1: I wanted to ask you about the Europeans because European nations have said they they couldn't back an agreement that didn't mention fossil fuels.
Hw much lobbying was happening behind the scenes to get them on board?
Speaker 2: Look, that there was an awful lot of lobbying going on, uh, all week, uh, even some head of government contacts as well, uh, to try and navigate this to a conclusion that could have included a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels.
Speaker 2: And that that failed.
Speaker 2: Um, why it failed, I think it's going to be picked apart for some time.
Speaker 2: I I my personal feeling is that the the way in which the presidency moved the politics forward in the last days had a bit of a tin ear to those countries that that are really important, the vulnerable countries, others who who needed to see this transition away from fossil fuel language.
Speaker 1: The draft acknowledges that the goal set by the 2015, uh, Paris agreement of keeping the rise in global temperatures below 1.5° is going to be missed.
How significant is that?
Speaker 2: Look, it's very significant.
Speaker 2: We've seen, you know, a massive amount of science this year coming out showing that the the the risks and damages of exceeding one and a half degrees are escalating quickly.
Speaker 2: But the focus now has to be to take action to limit the magnitude of that overshoot, the overshoot of 1.5, keep it as lowest possible, and get it down as fast as possible.
Speaker 2: In other words, limit the duration of that overshoot to minimize the damage, the damages are real.
Speaker 2: Um, we're already seeing really disastrous changes to our coral reefs as a consequence.
Speaker 2: 50,000 heat deaths in Europe this summer, attributable mostly to global warming, disaster in Nepal linked to climate change.
Speaker 1: The climate and energy Minister Chris Bowen, who's been leading these talks, uh, how have you judged his leadership of this forum?
Speaker 2: Look, my observation of, uh, Chris Bowen is he's put everything into this.
Speaker 2: He's done, you know, he's gone well above the call of duty to make this work.
Speaker 3: Um, so I I don't have a lot of, um, anything bad to say about that at all.
Speaker 3: I think he's done a a great job, very difficult political environment, very complicated situation, uh, with essentially a dual presidency, an experiment, I hope we never repeat again.
Speaker 3: At the end of the day, both Turkey and Australia have big interest in fossil fuels, and I think that began to come through in the last days here.
Speaker 1: In what way?
Speaker 3: Well, I I think there was a lot of countries that needed to see a transition away from fossil fuels.
Speaker 3: They didn't want to have this horrible language on carbon capture and storage.
Speaker 3: They didn't want to see the weakening of climate science, and that's what came through in the last 48 hours in the presidency text.
Speaker 3: I don't know which country, whether it was Turkey or Australia, responsible for that, but presidency text was not good, and that's why there was the explosion today that that killed this off.
Speaker 1: Is this a reputational blow for Australia as a climate leader?
Speaker 3: Look, Australia has a reputational problem because of its fossil fuel dependency, because of its ongoing development of fossil fuel projects at scale.
Speaker 3: There's roughly four climate bombs in the pipeline now in Australia.
Speaker 3: There's the Browse, uh, oil field, gas field off the West Australian coast, Scott Reef, there's a Valhalla fracking, um, and in the Kimberley, there's Beetu, and there's a coal mine in the Hunter Valley.
Speaker 3: So the the Australia has a big reputational problem that it needs to deal with.
Speaker 1: What does all this mean for Pacific nations, which Australia vowed to fight for at COP?
Speaker 3: They're very sad about the way things have turned out, actually.
Speaker 3: Um, when when I look at my mates, um, leaving today, they're feeling very sad and upset that we haven't made more progress on this.
Speaker 3: They really look to Australia for help, and they're feeling disappointed that we haven't been able to do enough as a country.
